issues.subcategory: contradictory effect size values across sections
issues.description: The original study's effect size for 'Advantageous' self-disclosure is reported inconsistently across the manuscript. In the abstract it is stated as -.30, in the Results section it is compared against -.30, but in Table 3 the original r is listed as -.33, and in the Discussion it is referenced as -.33. This discrepancy of .03 is non-trivial when the meta-analytic estimate is -.16 and the difference is being used to argue publication bias.
issues.quote: self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)... The effect sizes of all studies were descriptively less than or equal to the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.30)... [Table 3 shows original r = -0.33 for Advantageous]... the latter finding consistent with original study's larger susceptibility to publication bias than replication studies... (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)

issues.subcategory: contradictory direction of meta-analytic effect for connection
issues.description: The Results section states the meta-analytic point estimate for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' was .09 (positive), yet the original study found -.22 (negative), and the text states 'the summary estimate of the effect size was opposite in direction to the original in six of the seven replications.' However, the Discussion then states 'the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero' while also citing a PI of [-.07, .27]. But the Results section reports the meta-analytic p = .065 (not significant), directly contradicting the Discussion's claim that it was 'significantly different from zero.'
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065... [Discussion:] However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero. We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.

issues.subcategory: contradictory prediction intervals for connection outcome
issues.description: The prediction interval for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome is reported as [-.09, .26] in the Results section but as [-.07, .27] in the Discussion section. These are different values for the same statistic, indicating a transcription or calculation error in one of the locations.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065 [Results]... supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero [Discussion].

issues.subcategory: contradictory fail-safe number for connection outcome
issues.description: The Results section reports the FSN for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' as 5 studies, but the Discussion section refers to it as 11 studies. These are substantially different values that lead to different substantive conclusions about the stability of the finding.
issues.quote: The FSN was 5 studies [Results, Connect section]... These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies) [Discussion].

issues.subcategory: contradictory description of expression outcome FSN interpretation
issues.description: In the Discussion of the 'Opportunity to Express Self' outcome, the authors state 'The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.' However, the Results section reports the FSN as 3 (not 5), and a low FSN should reduce confidence in a significant finding, not increase confidence in a null finding. The logic is inverted: the FSN applies to the significant meta-analytic result (r=.08, p=.021), not to the null individual results.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies [Results]... The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications [Discussion].

issues.subcategory: incorrect equivalence of beta and r
issues.description: The authors state 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient' in the Table 1 note. This is only true in simple bivariate regression with a single predictor and when both variables are standardized. While this may hold approximately here given the simple regression design, the blanket equivalence claim is technically incorrect and could mislead readers. The original study used regression with potentially additional covariates, and the conditions under which beta = r must be explicitly verified and stated.
issues.quote: Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: sign inconsistency in Table 3 difference calculation for safety outcome
issues.description: In Table 3, for the Safety outcome, BYU-Sp16 shows replication r = 0.08 and original r = -0.31, with a listed difference of -0.39. The difference (replication minus original) should be 0.08 - (-0.31) = +0.39, not -0.39. The sign of the difference appears to be reversed. This same sign convention issue may affect interpretation of other rows in the table.
issues.quote: BYU-Sp16 | 0.08 | -0.31 | -0.39 | [ -0.66 , -0.09 ] [Safety section of Table 3]

issues.subcategory: inconsistent number of significant replications for connection outcome
issues.description: The Results section states 'six of the seven replication studies did not find self-esteem to be a significant predictor of opportunity to connect' (implying one did), and Table 1 shows SAU with p=.033 as the significant one. However, the text also states 'nonsignificant in all but one.' The Discussion then states the meta-analytic effect was 'significantly different from zero' when p=.065, which does not meet the conventional alpha=.05 threshold.
issues.quote: Contrary to the results of the original study, six of the seven replication studies did not find self-esteem to be a significant predictor of opportunity to connect... the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: original study beta for express not reported but effect size used
issues.description: Table 1 notes that the original study did not report a beta coefficient for the 'Express' variable (marked n/a*), yet Table 3 lists an original r of 0.15 for Express, and the Results and Discussion reference this value. The source and calculation method for this effect size are not explained, creating a transparency problem about how the original effect size was derived.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable. [Table 1 note]... BYU-Sp16 | 0.18 | 0.15 [Express section of Table 3]... Five of the seven studies showed an effect size descriptively smaller than the original study (.06 to .12 vs. .15)

issues.subcategory: missing information on how original effect sizes were calculated
issues.description: The authors state they calculated effect size r from t-statistics and degrees of freedom from the original study, but do not provide the formula used or verify these calculations against the original reported values. Given that the original study's beta for 'Express' was not reported, the derivation of r=.15 for that variable is entirely unexplained. The conversion formula and any assumptions made should be explicitly stated.
issues.quote: The original Forest and Wood (2012) regression results included t-statistics and degrees of freedom for all variables, so we chose to calculate effect size r for all four outcome variables in the study.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent measurement scale across replications
issues.description: Two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point RSE scale while the others used the original four-point scale. This is a meaningful methodological deviation that could affect the distribution and variance of self-esteem scores, and thus the regression coefficients. The authors acknowledge this but do not test whether scale format moderated results, nor do they discuss how this affects comparability of effect sizes across studies.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent data collection mode across replications
issues.description: Replications used different data collection modes (in-lab only, online only, or both), which is a known moderator of self-report responses, particularly for sensitive items related to self-esteem and social disclosure. Three used in-lab only, two online only, and two used both. This introduces systematic variance that is uncontrolled and untested as a moderator, potentially inflating heterogeneity estimates.
issues.quote: As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online, researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods).

issues.subcategory: group administration in one replication
issues.description: The SAU replication ran participants in groups of two to six, while all other replications ran participants individually. Group administration can introduce social desirability effects and demand characteristics, particularly for self-esteem measures and perceptions of social media. This is a meaningful procedural deviation that is not analyzed as a potential moderator.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent composite score calculation across replications
issues.description: The authors note that some studies mean-averaged items while at least one study (Gordon) appeared to sum items, based on the magnitude of reported means. This is a fundamental scoring inconsistency that would affect the scale of scores and potentially the regression coefficients, yet it is only mentioned as a caveat rather than being corrected or systematically addressed.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: missing data handling not reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe how missing data were handled in any of the seven replication studies or in the meta-analysis. Given that some studies collected data online (where dropout mid-survey is common) and others in-lab, and given that the authors acknowledge 'not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling,' this is a significant gap that affects reproducibility and validity.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: sample size range inconsistency
issues.description: The Methods section states 'Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374,' but Table 1 shows sample sizes of 90, 90, 80, 116, 94, 374, and 81 for the seven replications. The minimum is 80 (Gordon and SAU both have N=80), which is consistent, but the CREP minimum was stated as 120. Two studies (Gordon N=80, SAU N=81, BYU-Sp16 N=90, BYU-Wi17 N=90) fall below the stated minimum of 120, yet all are included without explanation.
issues.quote: The CREP team specified the minimum sample size required for the replication... set at 100 for larger studies... All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)... Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: misinterpretation of fail-safe number logic for null results
issues.description: The FSN analysis is designed to assess the robustness of a statistically significant meta-analytic result against publication bias by estimating how many null studies would be needed to render it non-significant. The authors misapply this logic to the 'Express' outcome by using a low FSN (3) to argue confidence in a null finding. A low FSN for a significant result (r=.08, p=.021) actually means the significant result is fragile, not that the null is robust. The conclusion drawn is the opposite of what the statistic supports.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: treating non-significant p-value as significant in discussion
issues.description: For the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome, the meta-analytic p-value is .065, which does not meet the conventional alpha = .05 threshold. Yet the Discussion states this effect was 'significantly different from zero,' which is incorrect under standard NHST conventions used throughout the paper.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065 [Results]... the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero [Discussion].

issues.subcategory: causal language from correlational/regression data
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, the authors use causal and predictive language (e.g., 'self-esteem predicts,' 'low self-esteem will feel safer') based on cross-sectional regression data. The original study and all replications are cross-sectional surveys, making causal inference inappropriate. The direction of causality between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions cannot be established from these data.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions... Future studies seem likely to find that self-esteem would predict users' perception that Facebook was more advantageous for self-disclosure than FTF.

issues.subcategory: undergraduate convenience sample generalizability overclaim
issues.description: All participants across all seven replications were undergraduate students at US universities, yet the introduction references 'two billion people worldwide' and '70% of the U.S. population' as the relevant population. The Discussion draws broad conclusions about Facebook users generally without adequately acknowledging that the findings may not generalize beyond college-aged US students.
issues.quote: Among social network sites, Facebook is a dominant platform that affects the thinking, emotions, behavior, and interactions of its active users, some two billion people worldwide, including 70% of the U.S. population... We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions.

issues.subcategory: Facebook perception measure not validated independently
issues.description: The Facebook perception measure was created by Forest and Wood (2012) and used without independent psychometric validation. The authors report internal consistency (alpha) but do not address construct validity, factorial structure, or whether the subscales measure distinct constructs. The connection subscale has notably lower reliability (α = .68-.84) and the measure has not been validated in populations other than the original sample.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012)... Subscale scores showed adequate to good internal consistency (expression: α ranged from .70 to .80; connection: .68 to .84; safety: .84 to .91; advantages: .89 to .94)

issues.subcategory: misapplication of social compensation theory
issues.description: The authors invoke social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000) as a framework, but this theory was developed in the context of internet use broadly and anonymous online interactions, not specifically Facebook, which is a non-anonymous, identity-linked platform. The application of social compensation theory to Facebook without addressing this distinction represents a theoretical mismatch, particularly since Facebook's non-anonymity may fundamentally alter the compensatory dynamics the theory predicts.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000; Wilson et al., 2012). This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc model selection without pre-registration
issues.description: The authors report comparing REML and DerSimonian-Laird models and selecting REML because it 'produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates.' This model selection decision appears to have been made after examining the data and is not described as pre-registered. Selecting among analytic models based on interpretability of results is a form of researcher degrees of freedom that could influence conclusions.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data.

issues.subcategory: heterogeneity statistics reported without adequate interpretation
issues.description: The I² statistic for Self-Disclosure Safety is 71.76%, indicating substantial heterogeneity, yet the authors state only 'some evidence of heterogeneity' and explicitly decline to explore moderators. Given that I²=71.76% suggests that the majority of variance is due to between-study differences rather than sampling error, this level of heterogeneity substantially undermines the interpretability of the pooled effect size and warrants more thorough investigation or at minimum stronger caveats.
issues.quote: The between-study variance showed some evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 18.69, p = 0.005; T2 = .02, 95% CI [0, .15]; I2 = 71.76%, 95% CI [27.06%, 94.69%]... we are reluctant to draw conclusive inferences from the heterogeneity statistics.

issues.subcategory: Table 2 contents not provided
issues.description: Table 2 is referenced in the Results section as showing 'each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables,' but the actual table contents are not included in the manuscript as provided. This prevents evaluation of baseline comparability across studies and replication of the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables. [Table 2 note:] Note. n/a = Data not available. n/c = Data not collected

issues.subcategory: exclusion criteria and data cleaning procedures not reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report any participant exclusion criteria (e.g., failed attention checks, incomplete responses, outliers) for any of the seven replication studies or for the meta-analysis. Given that some studies were conducted online where careless responding is more common, and that the authors acknowledge inconsistent documentation across studies, the absence of exclusion criteria reporting is a significant gap.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent description of original study findings
issues.description: The Introduction states the original study found that 'self-esteem did not predict participants' perceptions of Facebook as offering greater opportunities for self-expression,' implying a null result for expression. However, the original study's p-value for expression is listed as .181 in Table 1, which is indeed non-significant. But the original beta/r for expression is listed as 0.15 (positive direction), while the original study's hypothesis was that low self-esteem would predict greater expression (negative direction). The positive direction of the original effect is never discussed or reconciled with the theory.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not predict participants' perceptions of Facebook as offering greater opportunities for self-expression... [Table 1: Original Express p = .181, Table 3: Original Express r = 0.15 (positive)]

issues.subcategory: inadequate statistical power for individual replication studies
issues.description: The CREP minimum sample size was set at 120, yet four of the seven studies have sample sizes below 120 (Gordon N=80, SAU N=81, BYU-Sp16 N=90, BYU-Wi17 N=90). For detecting the original effect sizes (r ≈ -.22 to -.31) at 80% power with alpha=.05, approximately 82-165 participants are needed. Studies with N=80-90 are underpowered for the smaller effects, which inflates the rate of false negatives and makes individual study null results difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)... Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent description of CREP project name
issues.description: The manuscript refers to the project as both 'Collaborative Research and Education Project' and 'Collaborative Replication and Education Project' in different locations. The abstract and title use 'Replication' while the body text uses 'Research' in one instance. This is a minor but notable inconsistency in a paper about replication methodology.
issues.quote: several research teams at U.S. colleges and universities replicated the study as part of the Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP)... [Abstract:] Collaborative Replication and Education Project (CREP)

issues.subcategory: Facebook usage not measured or controlled
issues.description: None of the replication studies appear to have measured participants' actual Facebook usage frequency or engagement, which is a critical potential moderator and confound. Participants who rarely use Facebook cannot meaningfully assess its advantages for self-disclosure relative to FTF. The original study's approach to this issue is also not described, making it impossible to evaluate whether this confound was addressed.
issues.quote: participants completed the 10-item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSE; Rosenberg, 1965)... Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012).

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounds between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions
issues.description: The relationship between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions could be confounded by numerous third variables including social anxiety, introversion/extraversion, actual social network size, frequency of Facebook use, and age. None of these potential confounds are measured or discussed as alternative explanations for the observed associations, weakening causal inference claims.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.

issues.subcategory: prediction interval interpretation error for expression outcome
issues.description: The Discussion states 'the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study's' for the expression outcome. First, a prediction interval does not mean '95% of future studies will fall in this range' in the frequentist sense used here—it predicts where a single future study's effect size will fall with 95% probability. Second, the PI lower bound of .01 does not include zero, yet the authors simultaneously argue there is no effect, creating a logical contradiction.
issues.quote: the summary effect size was about half of the original's effect size, and the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study's, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study. The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect.

issues.subcategory: publication bias inference from PI without formal test
issues.description: The authors infer publication bias in the original study based on the observation that replication effect sizes are smaller than the original. While this pattern is consistent with publication bias, it is also consistent with regression to the mean, sampling variability, or genuine population differences between the original and replication samples. No formal test of publication bias (e.g., Egger's test, funnel plot asymmetry, p-curve analysis) is conducted, making the publication bias claim speculative.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study... the latter finding consistent with original study's larger susceptibility to publication bias than replication studies.

issues.subcategory: pre-registration details not centrally reported
issues.description: The manuscript states studies were pre-registered but provides only links to individual OSF pages rather than summarizing what was pre-registered (hypotheses, analysis plans, exclusion criteria, sample size justifications). Readers cannot evaluate adherence to pre-registration without accessing seven separate external documents. Key deviations from pre-registration, if any, are not reported.
issues.quote: This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page (for links to each project see https://osf.io/yb9cv/).
